Individual buyers are willing to pay a premium for perceived status even if alternatives exist.
predictions: If offered a lower-priced Neumann microphone marketed as a status item, purchase intent among individual buyers will be higher than for a comparable non-status branded microphone.
Surveyed buyers will cite "looking professional" or "showing expertise" as a reason for choosing Neumann over cheaper alternatives.

arguments.sample: 300 individual buyers and home-studio creators recruited via audio forums and social media, balanced between experienced and novice users
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (1-10 scale) and willingness to pay premium over a baseline price

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between status and performance frames is >= 1.5 points on the 10-point scale, proceed with differentiated proposition aligned with the higher-performing frame. If difference < 1.5 points, maintain single professional range.

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 self-identified boat owners (recruited via boating forums) and 100 homeowners with decks/fences (recruited via home improvement forums). Randomly assigned to view either a marine kit or a protective coating kit.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) measured as the maximum price participants would pay for the kit, and purchase intent (binary: would buy).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Boat owners will show WTP at least 20% above a baseline generic marine paint price and purchase intent >=30%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will show WTP at least 15% above a baseline generic exterior paint price and purchase intent >=30%.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed WTP for the assigned kit meets or exceeds the respective threshold (20% for marine, 15% for protective) AND purchase intent >=30%, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition. If either condition fails, reject that proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed DIY Kit Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for both marine and protective kits. If either kit meets its respective threshold (20% WTP premium and ≥30% purchase intent), proceed to develop that proposition; otherwise, reject it.
final.target_customer: Boat owners for marine kit; homeowners with decks/fences for protective coating kit
final.value_proposition: Premium, easy-to-apply branded kit that extends asset life and reduces maintenance effort, sold through Jotun’s existing retail network (Multicolor Centers)
final.next_action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online choice‑based conjoint survey (X1) with 200 participants (100 boat owners, 100 homeowners).
final.uncertainty: No public evidence currently demonstrates consumer demand or willingness to pay for a DIY marine or protective coating kit. Both theories remain unlikely until test results are available.
would_change_if: If the test shows WTP ≥20% premium and purchase intent ≥30% for the marine kit, T1 would become likely and we would develop the marine proposition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY boat owners will show a WTP premium of at least €10 (50% increase) for a marine coating marketed as premium, easy-to-apply, and time-saving.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP premium for the marine coating among DIY boat owners meets or exceeds €10, proceed to develop the differentiated marine proposition. If both meet the threshold, prioritize the segment with higher purchase intent. If neither meets the threshold, recommend no expansion.

T1.claim: DIY boat owners will adopt a differentiated consumer marine coating product if it is positioned as a premium, easy‑to‑apply solution that saves time and reduces professional service costs.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun would capture higher margins through premium pricing and direct‑to‑consumer sales; DIY boat owners benefit from lower total cost of ownership and convenience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: DIY boat owners currently rely on professional services for maintenance, which is costly and time‑consuming. A product that simplifies application and offers superior protection would shift their purchasing behavior from service contracts
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would sell the product through its existing Multicolor Centers and online channels, retaining brand control and earning premium prices compared to standard marine coatings.
assumptions: DIY boat owners represent a sizable, reachable segment within Jotun’s existing retail network.
They are willing to pay a premium for convenience and performance.
Jotun can adapt its marine coating formulation for consumer use without compromising performance.
predictions: If offered, at least 15% of surveyed DIY boat owners would indicate intent to purchase within 12 months.
Average willingness to pay would be at least 20% above current professional coating prices.

X1.name: Retail Channel Test for Marine and Protective Coatings
X1.method: Place limited stock of Jotun marine coating (for boat owners) and protective coating (for decks/fences) in selected Jotun Multicolor Centers. Track purchase intent and actual sales over 12 weeks.
X1.sample: 10 Multicolor Centers in Scandinavia with existing DIY traffic. Each center receives 20 units of marine coating and 20 units of protective coating.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured by a pre-purchase survey ("Would you buy this product?") and actual units sold per product type.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Marine coating purchase intent ≥ 30% and sales ≥ 10 units; protective coating purchase intent <20% and sales <5 units.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Protective coating purchase intent ≥ 25% and sales ≥ 10 units; marine coating purchase intent <20% and sales <5 units.

X1.decision_rule: If marine coating meets its threshold (intent ≥ 30% and sales ≥ 10) and protective coating does not (intent <20% or sales <5), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition for marine coatings. If protective coating meets its threshold and marine does not, recommend for protective coatings. If both meet thresholds, recommend both. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand for marine coatings or the effectiveness of retail channels. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Retail Channel Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and sales for marine and protective coatings in Multicolor Centers. If marine coating meets its threshold (intent ≥30% and sales ≥10 units), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for marine coatings; otherwise, maintain focus on B2B markets.
final.target_customer: DIY boat owners who currently purchase marine coatings from specialized suppliers and lack easy access to high‑performance coatings.
final.value_proposition: Offer Jotun marine coating through existing Multicolor Centers, providing convenient retail access to proven marine performance coatings, reducing search cost and positioning Jotun as the default choice for boat owners.
final.next_action: Implement the 12‑week test in 10 selected Multicolor Centers, tracking purchase intent surveys and actual unit sales for marine and protective coatings.
final.uncertainty: No public evidence currently demonstrates consumer demand for marine coatings through retail channels; the test is needed to validate demand and willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the test shows marine coating purchase intent below 30% or sales below 10 units, we would conclude there is insufficient demand to justify a differentiated consumer proposition and would recommend no expansion.
If protective coating meets its threshold while marine does not, we would shift focus to a consumer proposition for protective coatings instead.

arguments.name: Retail Channel Test for Marine and Protective Coatings
arguments.method: Place limited stock of Jotun marine coating (for boat owners) and protective coating (for decks/fences) in selected Jotun Multicolor Centers. Track purchase intent and actual sales over 12 weeks.
arguments.sample: 10 Multicolor Centers in Scandinavia with existing DIY traffic. Each center receives 20 units of marine coating and 20 units of protective coating.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured by a pre-purchase survey ("Would you buy this product?") and actual units sold per product type.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Marine coating purchase intent ≥ 30% and sales ≥ 10 units; protective coating purchase intent <20% and sales <5 units.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Protective coating purchase intent ≥ 25% and sales ≥ 10 units; marine coating purchase intent <20% and sales <5 units.

arguments.decision_rule: If marine coating meets its threshold (intent ≥ 30% and sales ≥ 10) and protective coating does not (intent <20% or sales <5), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition for marine coatings. If protective coating meets its threshold and marine does not, recommend for protective coatings. If both meet thresholds, recommend both. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for both marine and protective DIY kits. If the test meets the decision thresholds (≥40% intent and ≥20% premium for marine among boat owners, or ≥40% intent and ≥15% premium for protective among homeowners), proceed with the corresponding consumer 1.

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence available up to mid-2024.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Jotun’s current reach to individual buyers.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable evidence, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., DIY marine boat maintenance, residential protective coating for decks/fences).
2) Expand existing B2B offerings to include consumer-friendly packaging or distribution without a new product proposition.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B marine and protective coatings markets.
4) License Jotun’s marine/protective coating technology to third-party consumer brands for co‑branded products.

T1.claim: DIY boat owners will purchase Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, professional-grade solution that simplifies maintenance and protects their investment.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by capturing higher-margin consumer sales and building brand loyalty among boat owners.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners currently rely on specialized marine suppliers or generic paints; a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes professional performance and ease of use would shift them to buy directly from Jotun.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would sell through its existing Multicolor Centers and online channels at premium pricing, leveraging its marine coating expertise to command higher prices than standard DIY paints.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade marine coatings.
Jotun's marine coating technology is perceived as superior to generic alternatives.
Distribution through Multicolor Centers and online is sufficient to reach DIY boat owners.
predictions: If a test offers a limited-edition DIY marine coating kit at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard DIY paint.
Surveyed boat owners will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a product marketed as professional-grade marine coating.
T1.first_claim: DIY boat owners will purchase Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, professional-grade solution that simplifies maintenance and protects their investment.

T2.claim: Homeowners will purchase Jotun protective coatings for decks and fences if they view the product as a long‑term cost‑saving solution that reduces maintenance frequency and extends surface lifespan.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher‑margin protective coatings through its Multicolor Centers and online channels, capturing repeat purchases as surfaces require re‑coating every few years.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners currently use generic paints or hire professionals for deck/fence protection; a differentiated proposition emphasizing durability and lower total cost of ownership would shift them to buy Jotun directly.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would price protective coatings at a premium justified by extended service life, selling through existing retail and e‑commerce channels to capture recurring revenue from maintenance cycles.
assumptions: Homeowners calculate total cost of ownership and prefer products that reduce repainting frequency.
Jotun's protective coating technology delivers measurable durability advantages over generic alternatives.
Multicolor Centers and online platforms can effectively reach homeowners interested in deck/fence protection.
predictions: If a test offers a limited‑edition deck/fence protective coating kit marketed for long‑term savings, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard decorative paint.
Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a product positioned as a cost‑saving protective solution.

X1.name: DIY Marine vs Protective Coating Preference Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 DIY boat owners (recruited via boating forums and marine clubs) and 250 homeowners with decks/fences (recruited via home improvement platforms).
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") 2) Willingness to pay premium (percentage above standard DIY paint price). 3) Preference for product positioning (professional-grade vs cost-saving).

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY boat owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for the marine coating kit than homeowners do for the protective coating kit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for the protective coating kit than boat owners do for the marine coating kit.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for marine kit among boat owners >= 40% AND willingness to pay premium >= 20%, proceed with marine consumer proposition. Else if purchase intent for protective kit among homeowners >= 40% AND willingness to pay premium >= 15%, proceed with protective consumer proposition. Else no expansion.

arguments.claim: DIY boat owners will purchase Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, professional-grade solution that simplifies maintenance and protects their investment.
arguments.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by capturing higher-margin consumer sales and building brand loyalty among boat owners.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners currently rely on specialized marine suppliers or generic paints; a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes professional performance and ease of use would shift them to buy directly from Jotun.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would sell through its existing Multicolor Centers and online channels at premium pricing, leveraging its marine coating expertise to command higher prices than standard DIY paints.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade marine coatings.
Jotun's marine coating technology is perceived as superior to generic alternatives.
Distribution through Multicolor Centers and online is sufficient to reach DIY boat owners.
predictions: If a test offers a limited-edition DIY marine coating kit at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard DIY paint.
Surveyed boat owners will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a product marketed as professional-grade marine coating.

arguments.claim: Homeowners will purchase Jotun protective coatings for decks and fences if they view the product as a long‑term cost‑saving solution that reduces maintenance frequency and extends surface lifespan.
arguments.who_benefits: Jotun benefits by selling higher‑margin protective coatings through its Multicolor Centers and online channels, capturing repeat purchases as surfaces require re‑coating every few years.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners currently use generic paints or hire professionals for deck/fence protection; a differentiated proposition emphasizing durability and lower total cost of ownership would shift them to buy Jotun directly.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would price protective coatings at a premium justified by extended service life, selling through existing retail and e‑commerce channels to capture recurring revenue from maintenance cycles.
assumptions: Homeowners calculate total cost of ownership and prefer products that reduce repainting frequency.
Jotun's protective coating technology delivers measurable durability advantages over generic alternatives.
Multicolor Centers and online platforms can effectively reach homeowners interested in deck/fence protection.
predictions: If a test offers a limited‑edition deck/fence protective coating kit marketed for long‑term savings, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard decorative paint.
Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a product positioned as a cost‑saving protective solution.

arguments.name: DIY Marine vs Protective Coating Preference Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents: 250 DIY boat owners (recruited via boating forums and marine clubs) and 250 homeowners with decks/fences (recruited via home improvement platforms).
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") 2) Willingness to pay premium (percentage above standard DIY paint price). 3) Preference for product positioning (professional-grade vs cost-saving).

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY boat owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for the marine coating kit than homeowners do for the protective coating kit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for the protective coating kit than boat owners do for the marine coating kit.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for marine kit among boat owners >= 40% AND willingness to pay premium >= 20%, proceed with marine consumer proposition. Else if purchase intent for protective kit among homeowners >= 40% AND willingness to pay premium >= 15%, proceed with protective consumer proposition. Else no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for both marine and protective DIY kits. If the test meets the decision thresholds (≥40% intent and ≥20% premium for marine among boat owners, or ≥40% intent and ≥15% premium for protective among homeowners), proceed with the corresponding consumer 1.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home use, but first validate demand with a low‑cost messaging test. The evidence shows Tanita already markets a body‑fat analyser to professional users based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to disease, and the device is exempt from medical device regulation when used for non‑diagnostic purposes, indicating it can be positioned as a health‑monitoring tool

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser currently sold to clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; cannot use later events or internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for individual buyers.
Must consider alternatives including no expansion, redesigning the product, targeting a different customer group, or changing the distribution channel.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual consumers for home use (e.g., personal body‑fat monitoring).
2) Expand the existing BIA analyser to a broader B2B market (e.g., gyms, corporate wellness programs) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on clinic and health‑club sales.
4) Redesign the product for a different use case (e.g., medical diagnostics, fitness‑center equipment) and pursue a new distribution channel.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, driven by awareness of body-fat links to disease.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking health monitoring; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes, and cancers creates perceived health risk, motivating purchase of a tool to monitor body composition.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell a differentiated consumer model at higher margins through direct-to-consumer channels, leveraging its brand reputation for medical-grade accuracy.
assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita's medical-grade accuracy based on professional market presence.
Health awareness campaigns in 1993 effectively communicated disease links to body fat.
Price sensitivity is secondary to health concerns for target segment.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser if presented with medical risk information.
Willingness to pay will be above €100 for a device marketed as medically accurate.

Participants view a product description of a home body-fat analyser (Tanita brand) with either medical framing (health risk, disease prevention) or fashion framing (lifestyle accessory, status symbol). They then indicate purchase intent (1-10) and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers in Japan (target market) recruited via panel, balanced across age and gender. Randomly assigned 200 to medical framing, 200 to fashion framing.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-10) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: self-reported importance of health monitoring vs social signaling.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Medical framing group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than fashion framing group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fashion framing group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than medical framing group.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home use, but first validate demand with a low‑cost messaging test. The evidence shows Tanita already markets a body‑fat analyser to professional users based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to disease, and the device is exempt from medical device regulation when used for non‑diagnostic purposes, indicating it can be positioned as a health‑monitoring tool

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser currently sold to clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; cannot use later events or internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for individual buyers.
Must consider alternatives including no expansion, redesigning the product, targeting a different customer group, or changing the distribution channel.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual consumers for home use (e.g., personal body‑fat monitoring).
2) Expand the existing BIA analyser to a broader B2B market (e.g., gyms, corporate wellness programs) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on clinic and health‑club sales.
4) Redesign the product for a different use case (e.g., medical diagnostics, fitness‑center equipment) and pursue a new distribution channel.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes, and cancers creates perceived health risk, motivating purchase of a tool to monitor body composition.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can sell a differentiated consumer model at higher margins through direct-to-consumer channels, leveraging its brand reputation for medical-grade accuracy.
assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita's medical-grade accuracy based on professional market presence.
Health awareness campaigns in 1993 effectively communicated disease links to body fat.
Price sensitivity is secondary to health concerns for target segment.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser if presented with medical risk information.
Willingness to pay will be above €100 for a device marketed as medically accurate.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view a product description of a home body-fat analyser (Tanita brand) with either medical framing (health risk, disease prevention) or fashion framing (lifestyle accessory, status symbol). They then indicate purchase intent (1-10) and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers in Japan (target market) recruited via panel, balanced across age and gender. Randomly assigned 200 to medical framing, 200 to fashion framing.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-10) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: self-reported importance of health monitoring vs social signaling.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Medical framing group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than fashion framing group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fashion framing group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than medical framing group.

final.uncertainty: Actual consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home device; whether the medical framing resonates enough to justify investment; potential price sensitivity and competition from existing consumer scales

T1.claim: Recreational boaters will adopt a differentiated 406 MHz PLB if it is marketed as a safety essential for remote water activities, because they value personal safety and are willing to pay a premium for a device that meets regulatory requirements.
T1.who_benefits: ACR Electronics would benefit by capturing premium pricing and brand association with safety.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boaters currently use VHF radios and cell phones; a dedicated PLB offers a reliable, regulatory-compliant solution for emergencies, addressing a gap in safety equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price the PLB at $700 (as suggested in press release) and sell through specialty marine retailers, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Recreational boaters are aware of PLB regulations and seek compliant safety gear.
There is sufficient demand for a differentiated product beyond existing generic PLBs.
ACR can design a product that meets boater preferences (e.g., size, durability).
predictions: If offered, at least 10% of surveyed boaters would express intent to purchase within 12 months.
Sales would be concentrated in coastal states with high boater participation.

T2.who_benefits: ACR would benefit by selling PLBs through insurance channels at volume, potentially at lower margins but higher total sales.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Boaters currently purchase safety gear voluntarily; insurance mandates or subsidies lower the effective price and provide a clear incentive to adopt a compliant device.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell through insurance brokers or directly to insurers, capturing volume sales and possibly bundling with other marine safety products.
assumptions: Insurance regulators or insurers view PLBs as risk mitigation tools.
There is a market of insurers willing to offer subsidies or require PLBs for policyholders.
ACR can meet any insurance-specific requirements (e.g., durability, data reporting).
predictions: If offered, at least 15% of surveyed boaters with insurance would indicate they would purchase a PLB if their insurer required or subsidized it.
Sales would be higher in regions with higher marine insurance penetration.

X1.name: Boater Preference Survey with Insurance Incentive
X1.method: Online survey of recreational boaters in coastal states, presenting two product concepts: (1) a differentiated PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700; (2) the same PLB offered with a $200 insurance subsidy (effective price $500) and a statement that insurers may require it. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay. The survey also asks about current safety gear ownership and insurance status.
X1.sample: 500 recreational boaters recruited via boating clubs and marine forums, stratified by state (California, Florida, Washington) to reflect high boater participation. Recruitment cost estimated €2,000.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate for the differentiated product (T1) vs. purchase intent rate when insurance subsidy is offered (T2). Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the differentiated product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be at least 10% for the differentiated product at $700, and will not increase significantly when a subsidy is offered (difference <5 percentage points).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will increase by at least 10 percentage points when the insurance subsidy is offered, indicating that price reduction and insurer involvement drive adoption.

X1.decision_rule: If the purchase intent for the differentiated product at $700 is ≥10% AND the increase in intent when subsidy is offered is <5 percentage points, then T1 is supported and ACR should pursue a differentiated consumer proposition. If the increase is ≥10 percentage points, T2 is supported and ACR should explore insurance partnership. If neither condition is met, no expansion is recommended.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct the proposed Boater Preference Survey with Insurance Incentive (Test X1) to empirically test whether recreational boaters will purchase a differentiated PLB at $700 and whether insurance subsidies drive additional demand. final.value_proposition: A differentiated 406 MHz PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700, with optional insurance subsidy to lower effective price and potentially meet insurer requirements.
final.next_action: Run Test X1 (Boater Preference Survey with Insurance Incentive) within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget to measure purchase intent under differentiated pricing and insurance subsidy scenarios.
final.uncertainty: There is no public evidence that recreational boaters currently purchase PLBs or that they would pay $700 for a differentiated product. Insurance involvement is also unproven. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent ≥10% for the differentiated product at $700 and the subsidy does not increase intent by ≥10 percentage points, we would proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.

X1.name: Boater Willingness-to-Pay Survey with Insurance Subsidy Scenario
X1.method: Online survey of recreational boaters in the United States, recruited via boating forums and marine insurance provider lists. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Standard PLB description with suggested retail price $700; (2) Same description plus a statement that marine insurance companies offer a $200 discount for PLB ownership (effectively $500). Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay (WTP) and whether they would purchase. The survey also asks about insurance status (insured vs uninsured).
X1.sample: 400 boaters (200 per condition), balanced for region and experience level.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars and purchase intent (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP will be high (≥$500) regardless of subsidy, because boaters value safety and are willing to pay premium; purchase intent will be similar across conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP will be significantly higher in the subsidy condition (≈$500) than in the standard condition (≈$300), because the discount makes the device affordable; purchase intent will be higher among insured boaters in the subsidy condition.

X1.decision_rule: If average WTP in the subsidy condition is at least $450 and purchase intent among insured boaters in that condition exceeds 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition with insurance partnerships. If WTP in the standard condition is below $400, reject the premium pricing approach. If neither condition meets thresholds, decline expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct a targeted willingness-to-pay survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate demand and price sensitivity before committing resources. If the survey shows WTP ≥$500 and purchase intent ≥30% among insured boaters, proceed to develop a boater-focused PLB with insurance partnerships; otherwise, maintain focus on existing B2B markets.
final.target_customer: Recreational boaters who undertake remote trips and hold marine insurance.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated 406 MHz PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at a premium (e.g., $700) with optional insurance subsidy to lower effective cost, leveraging ACR's regulatory approval and brand association with safety
final.next_action: Run the proposed survey (400 boaters, two conditions) within 10 weeks, budget €15,000, to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent under standard and subsidy scenarios.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a premium-priced PLB among recreational boaters is unknown; willingness to pay and insurance subsidy impact are uncertain. No evidence currently supports T2 (insurance subsidy) or T1 (premium safety demand).
would_change_if: Survey shows average WTP ≥$500 and purchase intent ≥30% among insured boaters in the subsidy condition, indicating strong demand for a differentiated product.
New evidence emerges of insurance mandates or subsidies for PLBs, supporting T2.
Market research reveals existing consumer adoption of PLBs by boaters at premium prices, confirming T1.

arguments.name: Boater Willingness-to-Pay Survey with Insurance Subsidy Scenario
arguments.method: Online survey of recreational boaters in the United States, recruited via boating forums and marine insurance provider lists. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Standard PLB description with suggested retail price $700; (2) Same description plus a statement that marine insurance companies offer a $200 discount for PLB ownership (effectively $500). Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay (WTP) and whether they would purchase. The survey also asks about insurance status (insured vs uninsured).
arguments.sample: 400 boaters (200 per condition), balanced for region and experience level.
arguments.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars and purchase intent (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP will be high (≥$500) regardless of subsidy, because boaters value safety and are willing to pay premium; purchase intent will be similar across conditions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP will be significantly higher in the subsidy condition (≈$500) than in the standard condition (≈$300), because the discount makes the device affordable; purchase intent will be higher among insured boaters in the subsidy condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If average WTP in the subsidy condition is at least $450 and purchase intent among insured boaters in that condition exceeds 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition with insurance partnerships. If WTP in the standard condition is below $400, reject the premium pricing approach. If neither condition meets thresholds, decline expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct a targeted willingness-to-pay survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate demand and price sensitivity before committing resources. If the survey shows WTP ≥$500 and purchase intent ≥30% among insured boaters, proceed to develop a boater-focused PLB with insurance partnerships; otherwise, maintain focus on existing B2B markets.

arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated 406 MHz PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at a premium (e.g., $700) with optional insurance subsidy to lower effective cost, leveraging ACR's regulatory approval and brand association with safety
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed survey (400 boaters, two conditions) within 10 weeks, budget €15,000, to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent under standard and subsidy scenarios.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for recreational boaters, emphasizing the PLB as a safety necessity for remote water activities. Use the FCC approval and regulatory compliance as legitimacy signals, and price at the suggested $700 retail level. Begin with a limited launch through specialty marine retailers and direct-to-consumer channels to test demand before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment (e.g., market demand, competitive landscape, regulatory requirements, or existing consumer adoption).
Cannot rely on post‑2002 developments or later market outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., personal marine safety beacon for recreational boaters).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., sell existing 406 MHz beacons through retail channels to individual buyers).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Form partnerships with consumer brands to co‑brand a consumer‑focused beacon.

T1.claim: Recreational boaters will adopt a differentiated 406 MHz PLB if it is marketed as a safety necessity for remote water activities, because they value personal safety and are willing to pay a premium for a device that reliably alerts SAR.
T1.who_benefits: ACR Electronics would benefit by capturing premium pricing and brand association with safety.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boaters perceive the PLB as essential for life‑saving in remote environments, and regulatory approval (FCC waiver) signals legitimacy, prompting purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price the device above standard EPIRBs (e.g., $700 retail) and sell directly to consumers, retaining margin.
assumptions: Boaters are aware of the FCC approval and its safety implications.
There is sufficient demand among recreational boaters for a dedicated PLB.
ACR can reach this segment through retail or direct channels.
predictions: If offered a differentiated PLB, a sample of recreational boaters will express intent to purchase at the suggested retail price.
Sales will be higher than for a generic EPIRB sold through the same channel.
T1.first_claim: Recreational boaters will adopt a differentiated 406 MHz PLB if it is marketed as a safety necessity for remote water activities, because they value personal safety and are willing to pay a premium for a device that reliably alerts SAR.

T2.claim: Recreational boaters will adopt a differentiated 406 MHz PLB if it is marketed as a status symbol and fashion accessory, because they seek to display safety consciousness and differentiate themselves from peers, and are willing to pay a premium for a distinctive device.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Boaters view safety equipment as a way to signal responsibility and status; a unique design and branding make the PLB a conversation piece, prompting purchase beyond functional need.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price the device above standard EPIRBs and sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, retaining margin and brand equity.
assumptions: Boaters value visible safety gear as a status signal.
There is a segment willing to pay for distinctive design and branding.
ACR can create a differentiated aesthetic and marketing narrative.
predictions: If offered a differentiated PLB with unique design, a sample of boaters will express intent to purchase at the suggested retail price.
Sales will be higher than for a generic EPIRB sold through the same channel.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.
Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.
Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers.
T1.first_claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T2.claim: Professional landscapers and small farm operators will adopt garden tractors because they need reliable, efficient equipment for commercial work, and they value Deere's engineering reputation for durability and service support.
T2.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by selling higher-margin commercial-grade tractors and attachments through its dealer network, leveraging its established service infrastructure.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Commercial users require equipment that can handle continuous use and offers quick parts/service availability; Deere's reputation for robust engineering and dealer support makes it attractive.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.
assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.
Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.
Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated commercial garden tractor proposition, sales to professional landscapers will increase relative to competitors.
Commercial buyers will report higher satisfaction with Deere's service support compared to other brands.
Deere's dealer network will see increased service contract uptake from commercial customers.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.

Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.
assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.
Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.
Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 households with small gardens (verified by self‑report of garden size <0.5 acre) and 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators (verified by self‑report of commercial use). Randomly assign each respondent to either a consumer‑focused message (emphasizing low cost, ease of use, and suitability for small gardens) or a commercial‑focused message (emphasizing durability, service support, and suitability for professional work). After exposure, ask: "How likely are you to purchase a John Deere garden tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale. Also ask: "What is the maximum price you would pay?" and "Would you recommend this to others in your segment?". The test will be run in 12 weeks with a €20,000 budget for platform fees, incentives, and data analysis.
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 small‑garden households, 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators).
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each segment under each message condition.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional landscapers/small farm operators will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the commercial message than when exposed to the consumer message.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting households with small gardens, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network and engineering. The evidence shows rapid demand growth for garden tractors among small‑garden households who find them inexpensive, practical, and economical to maintain. Deere’s dealer network can reach these buyers without major new investment, and the company’s engineering reputation

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.
Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.
Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Commercial users require equipment that can handle continuous use and offers quick parts/service availability; Deere's reputation for robust engineering and dealer support makes it attractive.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.
assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.
Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.
Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated commercial garden tractor proposition, sales to professional landscapers will increase relative to competitors.
Commercial buyers will report higher satisfaction with Deere's service support compared to other brands.
Deere's dealer network will see increased service contract uptake from commercial customers.

Recruit 400 respondents: 200 households with small gardens (verified by self‑report of garden size <0.5 acre) and 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators (verified by self‑report of commercial use). final.target_customer: Households with small gardens (typically <0.5 acre) who need affordable, practical yard work solutions.
final.value_proposition: A Deere garden tractor marketed as a cost‑effective, easy‑to‑use solution for small gardens, sold through existing dealers with optional attachments (mowers, snow blowers).
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test to measure purchase intent differences and validate demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the small‑garden market and its willingness to pay a premium for Deere’s engineering are uncertain. Also uncertain is whether professional landscapers represent a larger or more profitable segment.
would_change_if: If the test shows that professional landscapers show a ≥1.5‑point higher purchase intent under a commercial message than under a consumer message, we would reconsider focusing on that segment.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 households with small gardens (verified by self‑report of garden size <0.5 acre) and 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators (verified by self‑report of commercial use). Randomly assign each respondent to either a consumer‑focused message (emphasizing low cost, ease of use, and suitability for small gardens) or a commercial‑focused message (emphasizing durability, service support, and suitability for professional work). After exposure, ask: "How likely are you to purchase a John Deere garden tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale. Also ask: "What is the maximum price you would pay?" and "Would you recommend this to others in your segment?". The test will be run in 12 weeks with a €20,000 budget for platform fees, incentives, and data analysis.
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 small‑garden households, 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators).
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each segment under each message condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Households with small gardens will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the consumer message than when exposed to the commercial message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional landscapers/small farm operators will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the commercial message than when exposed to the consumer message.

arguments.target_customer: Households with small gardens (typically <0.5 acre) who need affordable, practical yard work solutions.
arguments.value_proposition: A Deere garden tractor marketed as a cost‑effective, easy‑to‑use solution for small gardens, sold through existing dealers with optional attachments (mowers, snow blowers).

would_change_if: If the test shows that professional landscapers show a ≥1.5‑point higher purchase intent under a commercial message than under a consumer message, we would reconsider focusing on that segment.

If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two messages for either segment, we would conclude that a differentiated proposition is not justified and recommend no expansion.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners with small gardens, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network and engineering. The evidence shows rising homeownership and documented demand for inexpensive, practical garden tractors. A small‑farm proposition lacks supporting evidence and should be tested before investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing consumer sales through its existing dealer network and by leveraging its engineering to produce a differentiated garden tractor.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership rates in the 1950s-1960s increase the number of households with small gardens. These households seek practical, low‑maintenance solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need at an affordable price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell garden tractors through its independent dealer network, using the same engineering platform as farm tractors but scaled down. The value is captured through direct sales revenue and increased dealer traffic.
assumptions: Homeownership trends continue to rise, providing a growing base of potential buyers.
Garden tractors remain inexpensive and practical compared to manual tools.
Deere's dealer network can effectively reach individual homeowners.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor, sales will be positively correlated with regional homeownership rates.
Consumer surveys will show that price sensitivity and ease of use are primary purchase drivers for garden tractors.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T2.claim: Small‑farm operators will adopt a differentiated tractor proposition because they need a versatile, affordable machine that can replace multiple tools and reduce labor costs, and Deere can capture value by selling through its dealer network and offering financing.
T2.who_benefits: Deere & Company benefits by expanding its market beyond large farms to smallholders, increasing sales volume and dealer engagement.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Post‑war agricultural mechanization and rising labor costs make small farms seek equipment that can perform multiple tasks (plowing, planting, hauling) without requiring a large crew. A tractor that is cheaper than a full‑size farm tractor
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price a small‑farm tractor below its standard farm models, sell it through existing dealers, and offer financing to lower the entry barrier. Value is captured through higher unit volume and increased dealer traffic.
assumptions: Small farms constitute a sizable segment with unmet equipment needs.
Labor costs are rising enough to justify mechanization.
Deere's dealer network can reach small‑farm owners.
predictions: Sales of a differentiated small‑farm tractor will be higher in regions with a higher proportion of farms under 100 acres.
Purchasers will cite labor cost savings and task versatility as primary reasons for buying.
